title: Social teaching close
hookLine: love of neighbor, built into how we live together

cards: A bridge carries strangers across a river all day long, and hardly anyone crossing it thinks about it. Somebody did, once.
Somebody calculated the load, the wind, the winter, so that people they'd never meet could get home safely. That's care that doesn't look like care. It looks like steel and paperwork.
This block of the path began with a phrase, love, organized, and it ends today with a picture close to that bridge: love of neighbor, built into the way people live together.

teach.b: Start with the old command. Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." One person carrying another's load.
Catholic social teaching asks a second question: what if the load could be made lighter for everyone, before anyone has to carry it alone? Then two ways to love.

teach.h: FACE TO FACE, AND THROUGH INSTITUTIONS.
teach.b: Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote of the love of one neighbor, face to face, and also an institutional path of charity, where love works through law, economics and politics for the common good.
He called that second path no less a form of love than the first. Pope Francis, for his part, speaks of political love, the love that builds a fairer society for people one will never meet.
Then the block, added up. Every life. Everyone takes part.
Rights and duties. The poor first. Work has dignity.
One family. Our common home. Markets have limits.
Nothing and no one thrown away. Each one is love of neighbor, set into something that outlasts a single good deed.

teach.h: SO YOU SHALL FULFIL THE LAW OF CHRIST.
teach.b: Benedict was clear that no structure will ever make person-to-person love unnecessary. There will always be someone lonely, someone grieving, someone who needs a face, not a policy.
So the Church asks for both: the hand on the shoulder, and the bridge. Love made structural isn't love made cold. It's love that keeps working after you've gone home.

how: Catholics live social teaching both in direct works of mercy and in longer commitments: volunteering on a schedule, giving regularly, joining parish justice groups, and taking part in public life with the Church's principles in mind.

o: the block's summing-up: love built into shared life
the final papal letter on social questions
a teaching kept close and private to oneself

games.q: social teaching close — tap the pairs.

s: Benedict XVI called working through laws and institutions a lesser kind of love
he called the institutional path no less a form of charity than the face-to-face kind.
the Church teaches that good structures can make person-to-person love unnecessary
Benedict was clear there will always be people who need a face, not a policy.
Pope Francis speaks of political love
the love that builds a fairer society for people one will never meet.

games.q: your street floods every spring and the same neighbors lose everything. you've helped bail out basements for years. what does love made structural add?
o: keep helping, and push for a drain that stops the flood.
games.why: the Church asks for both: the hand on the shoulder now, and the structure that lightens the load for everyone.

practice: Let a few of the block's lines pass slowly, the poor first, our common home, everyone takes part, and notice which one stays.

Then picture one small act tied to it that could keep going without deciding it fresh each time: a monthly gift, a regular shift, a reminder to write to your representative again. If you pray, offer it to God as a promise.

wordCard.voice: Social teaching close. The block in one picture: love of neighbor, face to face and built into how people live together. Tomorrow a new block begins, on Mary: her feasts, her titles, and what the Church teaches about her.

carryVoice: Your line: love made structural. A hand on the shoulder, and a bridge. That's the block; see you for Mary tomorrow.
